analysis.one_liner: Triples court damages for people hurt by products that violate federal consumer safety standards.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to two House committees in November 1999 and died there when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Anyone suing over an injury caused by a product that did not meet a Consumer Product Safety Commission standard — whether that standard was mandatory or voluntary — would automatically recover three times their damages. The bill also required the Commission to reissue all of its product standards with a notice telling manufacturers about the new treble-damages rule within 90 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers injured by products that violate CPSC safety standards would see their lawsuit recoveries tripled, giving them and their lawyers a much stronger incentive to sue over unsafe products. Stronger lawsuits would also push manufacturers to design products that actually meet the safety standards rather than risk large payouts.

how_it_helps.text: A person injured by a product that fails to meet any CPSC standard, mandatory or voluntary, would recover treble damages in federal or state court, not just ordinary compensation.

The Consumer Product Safety Commission would have to reissue every one of its existing product standards within 90 days with a notice telling manufacturers that violations now carry treble damages, so no company could claim it was unaware of the penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of consumer products covered by CPSC standards, which would face tripled payouts when their products violate a standard and get injured people's lawsuits. Some of that cost would likely be passed along in prices, and companies facing treble exposure would have a strong incentive to fight even valid claims harder.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes treble damages automatic — a court 'shall' award them — leaving no room for a judge to consider whether the violation was minor, technical, or barely connected to the injury, so a trivial defect could still produce a tripled payout.

It applies to voluntary standards as well as mandatory ones; voluntary standards are often technical and change frequently, which could expose companies to tripled liability for falling short of benchmarks they were never legally required to meet.

Tripled liability across the consumer product sector would raise litigation costs, which manufacturers would partly pass to consumers in prices and partly spend on fighting claims rather than on safety improvements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Tripling damages for products that violate safety standards is a real deterrent that would likely make products safer and give injured people meaningful compensation, but the automatic, no-discretion trebling — including for violations of voluntary standards — is blunt and would invite fights over technical defects. A version that gave judges discretion would have preserved the deterrent with less cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Judiciary and Commerce committees, then a subcommittee, and never came back out for a House vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill in the House on November 18, 1999.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Commerce Committee for consideration of provisions within each panel's jurisdiction.
On December 3, 1999, the portion under Judiciary's jurisdiction was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, where it stayed.
The bill attracted no cosponsors, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer product manufacturers are better off, since they face only ordinary damages rather than tripled payouts when products violate CPSC safety standards. Injured consumers are left with the existing, smaller remedies.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the treble-damages bill and referred it to two committees; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection and took no further action on it.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for consideration of provisions in its jurisdiction and took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern on the merits can be read from the record; the sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.note: Companies selling products covered by CPSC standards would face tripled damages whenever a product injures someone while out of compliance, including under voluntary standards. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against injured consumers' interest in bigger recoveries.

Larger automatic recoveries would make CPSC-standard violations far more valuable to sue over, expanding work and fees for consumer-injury lawyers. That financial incentive lines up with injured consumers' ability to hold manufacturers accountable.
